title: Two curves, and where they touch

cues.text: Everything so far was about the chance to build, which pays you nothing while you hold it.
A project that has actually been built is different. It hands you the money coming in, every year, while you own it. So the balance has one more thing on it.
Which is the same equation with a single extra R on the end — the revenue it pays out. That is equation A five.

Its answer is the plain worth of the revenue stream, plus a term that is the value of the option to give up. That option is worthless when takings are enormous, which is what fixes which power survives this time.
Here is what waiting is worth: B times R to the beta, the curve we just derived.
And here is what a running project is worth, once you allow it to be abandoned. Nearly a straight line when takings are high, bending away as they fall.
At the level where she builds, stepping from one curve to the other must be worth exactly the cost of building. Not more, or she would have built sooner. Not less, or she would not build at all.
And a second condition, which is the subtle one. The two curves must not just be the right distance apart — they must have the same steepness there. They meet tangentially.
Because a corner would mean the trigger was in the wrong place: nudge it either way and you would do better. Only where the slopes agree is there nothing left to gain.
smooth pasting. Where two value curves meet, their slopes must agree.
At the build line, the step up is worth the cost.
And the slopes agree there.
At the give-up line, the step is worth nothing at all — she simply walks away.
And the slopes agree there too.
Four conditions. Four unknowns: the two amounts, and the two levels.

And the paper is honest about what happens next. There is no formula. The four have to be solved together on a computer. Which is exactly why the two numbers chapter thirteen ended on were printed rather than derived: nought point seven two, and one point six two.
